# The Brass Machine That Knew the Future

In the early 1870s William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, designed a machine that could tell you the height of the sea at a given harbor at any hour of any day in the coming year. It was made of brass wheels, pulleys, and one long wire, and its descendants stayed in service for nearly a century. I think it is one of the most satisfying objects ever built, and I want to explain why.

Start with the problem. Tides are driven by the moon and sun, whose motions are known with great precision. But you can't calculate the tide at Liverpool from astronomy alone, because the water has to slosh across the real Atlantic, around the real Ireland, and up the real Mersey, and the geometry of all that is far too complicated to work through from first principles.

The insight was that the problem splits in two. Astronomy supplies a list of rhythms. The moon raises a tide roughly every 12 hours and 25 minutes, the sun raises one every 12 hours, and the moon's changing distance and the tilt of its orbit add slower cycles. Each of these contributes a pure oscillation at an exactly known frequency. The harbor decides how strongly it responds to each rhythm and with how much delay. Those numbers can't be derived, but they can be measured: record the water level for a year and find the amplitudes and timings that fit.

The tide at any place is then a sum of a few dozen sine waves, with the frequencies taken from the heavens and the weights taken from the place. Familiar tidal behavior falls out of the sum. The lunar and solar rhythms drift in and out of step every two weeks, which is why tides swing between large spring ranges and small neap ones.

Adding dozens of sine waves by hand for every hour of a year is miserable work, so Kelvin mechanized it. Each rhythm gets a wheel, geared to turn at the correct speed relative to the others, with a pin set off-center by a distance matching that rhythm's strength at the harbor in question. Each pin moves a pulley up and down. A single wire, anchored at one end, threads over and under every pulley, and its free end carries a pen. Because the wire has a fixed length, the pen moves by the total of all the pulley motions. Turn the crank, let paper roll past, and the pen draws the tides. Kelvin's first machine combined ten rhythms and produced a year of predictions in about four hours.

The most consequential use of such a machine came in 1944. Arthur Doodson ran the Liverpool Tidal Institute from an observatory at Bidston, across the Mersey from the city, and was probably the world's leading authority on tidal analysis. In late 1943 the Admiralty asked him for predictions for a stretch of coast identified only by a code name. The constants he was given had been partly pieced together from sparse measurements, since nobody could set up a tide gauge on a beach in occupied France. He and his staff ran their two machines for long hours and produced the tables for Normandy.

The tide mattered because of Rommel. He had covered the beaches with steel and timber obstacles, many of them mined, positioned to sit hidden just under the surface at high water. He expected the Allies to land at high tide, when the exposed beach the troops had to cross would be narrowest. The Allied planners chose instead to land soon after low water on a rising tide, so the obstacles would be visible, engineers could clear lanes through them, and landing craft could float off again instead of stranding. They also wanted that tide to arrive shortly after dawn, following a night with enough moonlight for the airborne troops. Those conditions coincided on only a few days each month. For June 1944 the candidates were the 5th, 6th, and 7th, and that had been settled months in advance.

What could not be settled in advance was the weather. In the first days of June, Eisenhower's meteorologists, led by James Stagg, argued among themselves about a storm moving in from the Atlantic. They could see a day or two ahead, with difficulty. Stagg advised that the 5th would be impossible and that a gap in the weather might open on the 6th. Eisenhower postponed by twenty-four hours on the strength of that forecast, and the gap opened.

I keep coming back to this pairing. The same operation depended on two predictions about the same sea and sky. One could be made months ahead, and in principle decades ahead, by a crank-driven brass instrument. The other could barely be made two days ahead by the best forecasters alive, and cannot be made two weeks ahead today with supercomputers.

The difference has nothing to do with effort or computing power. It lies in the kind of system each one is. The tide is pushed by clockwork, and the ocean responds to that push in a nearly proportional way, so a small error in the inputs stays a small error in the output indefinitely. The atmosphere amplifies its own small differences, so any error in the starting picture grows until it swamps the forecast. No amount of brass or silicon gets you past that.

So how far ahead you can see depends mostly on what you are looking at. The tide happens to be one of the few natural phenomena that affects daily life and is also built almost entirely from cycles.

What I admire in Kelvin's approach is the division of labor. He never solved the ocean. He worked out which part of the problem theory could supply exactly and which part had to be asked of each harbor by watching it, and then built something that combined the two. The messy physics of coastlines never had to be understood, only measured once and encoded as the positions of a few pins.

The method has outlived the machines. The American tide predictor completed in 1910, known as Old Brass Brains, summed 37 rhythms and ran until 1965. The official United States tide tables are now computed in software, and the standard calculation still sums 37.
